# 2016 Nissan Altima Making Noise While Cold When Reversing

A squeaky clacking noise originating from the passenger side glove box area of a 2016 Nissan Altima, specifically when the vehicle is cold and in reverse, points to a thermal expansion issue involving the HVAC system or dashboard assembly. The symptom profileânoise occurring only during cold starts and ceasing once the engine warms upâis the critical diagnostic clue here.

When a car sits overnight, metal components contract. As the engine runs and coolant temperature rises, these parts expand. If a plastic clip, trim piece, or bracket has become loose enough that it can rattle against a moving component when cold, the friction creates an audible squeak or clack. Once thermal equilibrium is reached, the clearance changes, and the noise stops.

The specific location describedâglove box area during reverseâsuggests interaction between the HVAC blower motor assembly, the fresh air intake ducting, or the dashboard mounting points. In many Nissan models of this generation, the fresh air intake hose runs near the passenger side footwell and connects to the heater core assembly. If the heat shield for the exhaust manifold (which is located on the passenger side) has shifted slightly due to age or previous repairs, it could be vibrating against a plastic bracket when the engine torque changes during gear shifts.

However, the most likely culprit for noise localized near the glove box that disappears as the cabin warms is a loose interior trim piece or a failed HVAC actuator arm. The blend door actuators in these vehicles can become brittle over time. When cold, the plastic gears inside the actuator may not mesh perfectly, allowing the door to flop against the firewall or heater box casing when the blower fan engages. As the unit heats up and the plastic softens slightly, or as the metal housing expands, the fit becomes tighter, eliminating the rattle.

To diagnose this without disassembling the entire dash, start by locating the fresh air intake duct. This is a large black plastic hose that runs from the cabin filter area toward the heater box. Check for any loose clamps or disconnected sections that might be vibrating against the metal HVAC housing. If you find a gap where two plastic pieces meet, you can often secure it temporarily with a small amount of high-temperature silicone sealant or by adding a rubber grommet to dampen the vibration.

If the noise persists after checking external ducts, the issue may lie with the blower motor resistor or the motor housing itself. The resistor sits in close proximity to the heater core and can vibrate against the metal casing if its mounting bolts have worked loose. A simple torque check on these fasteners often resolves the rattle without requiring a full removal of the glove box assembly.

Another possibility involves the rearview mirror mount or the sun visor hinge, which are located directly above the glove box area. While less common to cause a "clacking" sound specifically tied to reverse gear engagement, the shift in engine torque when shifting into reverse can transmit enough vibration through the chassis to agitate loose fasteners anywhere on the passenger side upper dash. Inspect all visible screws and clips in that region for signs of wear or stripped heads.

If none of these mechanical adjustments resolve the issue, consider the possibility of a failing HVAC control panel. The buttons and sliders on the climate control interface can sometimes rub against the trim housing if the panel has sagged over time. A slight repositioning or replacement of the mounting clips might be necessary to restore a tight fit.

Addressing this issue early prevents minor rattles from developing into more significant structural issues, such as broken plastic clips that require full dashboard removal for repair. Monitoring the noise pattern as the car warms up provides valuable data on whether the problem is purely thermal expansion or if there is underlying wear in the HVAC mechanical components.
